ety.text: From Middle French vague, from Latin vagus (“uncertain, vague”, literally “wandering, rambling, strolling”).

senses.d: Not clearly expressed; stated in indefinite terms.
Not having a precise meaning.
Not clearly defined, grasped, or understood; indistinct; slight.
ex: only a vague notion of what’s needed
a vague hint of a thickening waistline

senses.d: Not clearly felt or sensed; somewhat subconscious.
Not thinking or expressing one’s thoughts clearly or precisely.
ex: Waxed-fleshed out-patients / Still vague from accidents, / And characters in long coats / Deep in the litter-baskets […]

senses.d: Lacking expression; vacant.
Not sharply outlined; hazy.
Wandering; vagrant; vagabond.
ex: The Lord Gray incourag'd his men to set sharply upon the vague villains
She danced along with vague, regardless eyes, / Anxious her lips, her breathing quick and short: [...]

senses.d: An indefinite expanse.
ex: The gray vague of unsympathizing sea / That dragged his fancy from her moorings back / To shores inhospitable of eldest time.

senses.d: A wandering; a vagary.
ex: [T]he Scots had some leasure to plaie their vagues

senses.d: to wander; to roam; to stray.
To become vague or act in a vague manner.
ex: Vaguely, yes. I've vagued all my life; that's been my curse.
A man's mind vagued up a little, for how can you remember the feel of pleasure or pain or choking emotion?

senses.d: To make vague negative comments publicly; to make highly veiled complaints or insults.

grp.label: not clearly defined, grasped, or understood
not thinking or expressing one’s thoughts clearly or precisely

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French vague, borrowed from Latin vagus (“uncertain, vague”, literally “wandering, rambling, strolling”). Possibly a doublet of gai.

chain.g: wandering, rambling, strolling, roving, roaming, unfixed, unsettled, vagrant

ety.text: Latin vāgīnalbor. English vagina Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīna (“sheath”).

senses.d: A sex organ for copulation and birth, found in female therian mammals, consisting of a passage between the vulval vestibule and the cervix of the uterus.
A similar organ in some invertebrates and non-mammalian amniotes.
A sheathlike structure, such as the leaf of a grass that surrounds a stem.
The vulva, or the vulva and vaginal passage collectively.
ex: For quotations using this term, see Citations:vagina.

senses.d: A coward; a weakling; a pussy.
ex: 2002, "The New Terrance And Phillip Movie Trailer" (South Park TV episode)

senses.d: The anus.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin vāgīna. Compare the inherited doublet gaine. Compare also gouine, which may be borrowed from Breton gouin, itself ultimately borrowed from the Latin. Also a doublet of gaine (“sheath”), which was inherited from the Latin.
Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīna. Doublet of guaina.
Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīna. Doublet of vaina.
Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīna. Doublet of bainha and vagem.
Inherited from Latin vāgīna (with change of /w/ to /ɡw/ influenced by Germanic). Compare French gaine, Spanish vaina, Sicilian vajina, Portuguese bainha. Doublet of vagina.

senses.d: In a vague manner.
ex: He looked vaguely around the room, as if lost.
The youth pointed vaguely. "Over there," he replied.

senses.d: Loosely; more or less; somewhat.
